prompt: Of the four numbers read off a request profile, which one does Lambda's bill follow, at a fixed duration and memory size?
hint: Lambda pays per request and per GB-second of each request.

choices.text: The peak hour
choices.why: The peak sizes instances and tasks. A function adds environments as requests arrive and pays for none in advance.

choices.text: The number of idle hours
choices.why: Idle hours cost a function nothing, so they are where it gains, but they do not set its bill.

choices.text: The volume
choices.why: Right: how many requests arrive in the month. With duration and memory fixed, the bill is the volume times a price per request.

choices.text: The hour of the day the traffic starts
choices.why: A function is billed the same at 03:00 as at 15:00.

prompt: A service takes 20 requests a second for 12 hours a day and none in the other 12. Over the average month of 730 hours (30.42 days), how many requests is that, in millions, to two decimal places?
hint: Requests a day, then times 730 / 24.

prompt: The office profile carries 59.13 million requests a month, which averages 22.5 a second. Why is the average the wrong number to price it with?
hint: Which two numbers does an average flatten?

choices.text: It hides the peak of 60 and the 15 silent hours
choices.why: Right. Containers are sized for the peak, and a function and App Runner gain from the silent hours; two services with the same average can need opposite answers.

choices.text: It is wrong arithmetic: 59.13 million a month is closer to 60 a second
choices.why: The arithmetic holds: 59.13 million over 2,628,000 seconds is 22.5. The trouble is what it leaves out.

choices.text: Averages are in requests a second, and AWS prices by the hour
choices.why: Units convert. The problem is the shape of the day, which no conversion brings back.

choices.text: The average ignores the request duration
choices.why: Neither the average nor the profile carries duration; it is the fourth number, read separately.

prompt: Concurrency, the number of requests in flight at once, is the rate of requests multiplied by their ___.
hint: Lesson 16 used Little's law: 60 a second at 100 ms each is six at once.

prompt: Match each number read off a request profile to the part of the bill it drives.
hint: Which meter or which sizing decision does each one feed?

pairs.right: How many instances or tasks must run
Where App Runner pays memory alone
The GB-seconds, and which timeouts apply

right_distractors: The tax rate of the region

prompt: In compare.py's table, App Runner is the cheapest option for the office profile, at 27.74 USD. What makes it cheaper there than on the steady profile?
hint: Count the hours with no request.

choices.text: Office has fewer requests in the month
choices.why: App Runner does not bill per request; 59.13 against 78.84 million is not what moves its column.

choices.text: Its 15 idle hours a day pay memory only, not the processor
choices.why: Right. Steady has no idle hour, so it pays both meters around the clock: 56.94.

choices.text: App Runner charges its us-east-1 price only during office hours
choices.why: The us-east-1 price applies to every row alike.

choices.text: Its peak of 60 is lower than the steady profile's
choices.why: The office peak of 60 is the higher of the two; steady runs at 30.

prompt: In compare.py, change MS from 100 to 200 and keep everything else. Two Fargate tasks still cost 49.596 USD a month; a request now costs 0.2 USD per million plus 0.1 GB-second at 0.0000133334. At how many million requests a month does Lambda cost the same as the two tasks? Two decimal places.
hint: Price per request first, then divide the tasks' month by it.

prompt: EC2 shows the same 162.21 USD on every row of compare.py's table, and is the dearest option on three of the four. What is the table telling you?
hint: How much traffic do two c7g.large serve before a third is needed?

choices.text: That the sheet's EC2 prices for São Paulo are wrong, too high for this machine
choices.why: The price is the sheet's, 0.1111 an hour; nothing about it is wrong.

choices.text: That instances do not scale, so the program is unable to add one when traffic grows
choices.why: The program sizes instances hour by hour like everything else; up to 400 a second, two are enough.

choices.text: That a small service cannot fill the smallest instance worth running
choices.why: Right. Two machines of 2 vCPU are capacity for 400 a second, and only the busy profile fills them.

choices.text: That EC2 bills per request at a higher rate than Lambda
choices.why: EC2 bills by the hour whatever the requests; that is exactly why the figure never moves.

prompt: Which of these does compare.py leave out of its prices? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about what sits in front of the compute, and what a contract changes.

choices.text: The load balancer that EC2 and Fargate need in front of them
choices.why: Its price is not on this course's sheet; aws-foundations lesson 22 prices it.

choices.text: Savings Plans and Reserved Instance discounts
choices.why: The sheet is on-demand list prices only.

choices.text: Lambda's price per million requests
choices.why: It is in: 0.2 USD per million, read from the sheet.

choices.text: The minutes an auto scaling group takes to react
choices.why: The program sizes every hour perfectly, which a real group never does.

choices.text: Fargate's memory price
choices.why: It is in: 0.00612 USD per GB-hour on Arm, read from the sheet.

prompt: With compare.py's assumptions, a request runs 100 ms in a 512 MB function on Arm. At 0.2 USD per million requests and 0.0000133334 USD per GB-second, what does one million requests cost, in USD, to four decimal places?
hint: One request is 0.1 s × 0.5 GB of GB-seconds.

prompt: According to the API documentation for create-function, how long may an ordinary Lambda function run before it is stopped?
hint: The default is 3 seconds; the question is the ceiling.

choices.text: 29 seconds
choices.why: That is a REST API integration's default timeout in API Gateway, not the function's.

choices.text: 900 seconds
choices.why: Right: fifteen minutes. A job longer than that has to be split, moved to a task, or orchestrated.

choices.text: 30 seconds
choices.why: That is the most an HTTP API integration waits.

choices.text: One hour, 3,600 seconds
choices.why: No such limit is documented for an ordinary function; 900 seconds is the ceiling.

prompt: An export endpoint takes 45 seconds to answer. The team wants to put it on Lambda behind an HTTP API. What has to change?
hint: Which limit is shorter here, the function's or the integration's?

choices.text: Nothing; 45 seconds is well inside Lambda's fifteen minutes
choices.why: The function would finish, but the HTTP API stops waiting at 30 seconds, and the caller gets an error.

choices.text: Raise the HTTP API integration timeout to 60 seconds
choices.why: An HTTP API integration allows 30 seconds at most. Only REST APIs, Regional or private, can go past 29.

choices.text: Turn it into a queued job the client collects later
choices.why: Right: accept the request, queue the work, and let the client collect the result. The request returns at once, and the 45 seconds happen outside any integration timeout.

choices.text: Give the function more memory so it answers within the limit
choices.why: More memory buys more CPU and might shorten it, but nothing says it reaches 30 seconds; the design should not depend on it.

prompt: The 45-second export becomes a job. Put the steps in the order they happen.
hint: The caller hears back first; the work comes after.
items: The API accepts the request and answers with a job id
A message describing the export goes onto a queue
A worker takes the message and builds the export
The client asks for the job and downloads the result
trap: Building the export before answering is the synchronous endpoint again, and the 30-second limit with it.

prompt: moto created a function with --timeout 901 and an HTTP API integration of 120,000 ms without complaint. What should you conclude?
hint: Who enforces a limit: the imitation, or the service?

choices.text: AWS has raised both limits, and moto follows its newest model
choices.why: The command line's own model still documents 900 seconds and 30,000 ms. moto simply does not check.

choices.text: The limits apply only in us-east-1
choices.why: Nothing in the documentation ties them to a region; moto would accept the same values anywhere.

choices.text: moto skips these checks; AWS refuses both calls
choices.why: Right, and the limit has to be read in the documentation. A limit met only in an imitation is a limit not yet met.

choices.text: The AWS CLI rewrote the values to legal ones before sending them
choices.why: moto answered 901 and 120000 back; the values went through unchanged.

prompt: A Lambda function's /tmp is 512 MB by default and can be configured up to ___ MB, according to the API's documentation.
hint: Ten gigabytes, written in megabytes.

prompt: For the shop's profile, App Runner comes out at 56.94 USD, the same as for the steady profile. Why does it not gain from the shop's quiet nights?
hint: Look at the rate between midnight and 07:00.

choices.text: The nights are not quiet: 2 requests a second keep its instances active, so the processor is billed all night
choices.why: Right. With silent nights the same profile costs 41.37.

choices.text: App Runner bills by the month, whatever the traffic
choices.why: It bills memory and processor by the hour; the 41.37 of silent nights proves the traffic matters.

choices.text: The evening peak of 80 needs a third instance all day
choices.why: Two instances serve up to 100 a second in the program, so 80 fits in the two it keeps.

choices.text: App Runner's us-east-1 price rises at night
choices.why: There is one price per meter, at any hour.

prompt: compare.py prices the shop at 56.94 USD on App Runner with a trickle of 2 a second at night, and at 41.37 USD with silent nights. How much does the trickle cost a month, in USD?
hint: A subtraction.

prompt: Which number, written down beside the shop's decision, would reopen it in favour of Lambda?
hint: The last line of compare.py.

choices.text: An evening peak that climbs above 100 requests a second for an hour
choices.why: A higher peak adds tasks and makes the containers dearer, but it is not the break-even with Lambda.

choices.text: Average traffic staying below about 21.8 requests a second
choices.why: Right. Below that, a function costs less than the two tasks the shop keeps.

choices.text: Traffic growing towards 400 a second
choices.why: That reopens it in favour of instances and a Savings Plan, as the busy row shows.

choices.text: The report taking longer than six minutes
choices.why: The report decides where the report runs, not where the API runs.

prompt: The six-minute sales report fits inside Lambda's fifteen minutes. Why did the shop run it as a scheduled Fargate task instead?
hint: What already exists, and what would have to be built?

choices.text: Lambda refuses jobs started by a schedule
choices.why: A schedule can invoke a function; that is a common use of one.

choices.text: A Fargate task is free when it runs only once a night
choices.why: It is billed for the minutes it runs, like every task.

choices.text: It reuses the image the API already builds, so nothing new has to be packaged
choices.why: Right. Both would work; the task costs the shop no new packaging and no new skill.

choices.text: Six minutes is over the HTTP API's 30 seconds
choices.why: The report is not called through an API at all; that limit does not touch it.

prompt: A webhook receiver gets about 5,000 calls a day, at random hours, each running 200 ms. Nobody knows when the next one comes. Which option does this lesson's arithmetic point to?
hint: Volume, peak and idle hours: which of them is large here?

choices.text: Two Fargate tasks, for availability
choices.why: Two tasks cost 49.60 a month to wait for 5,000 calls a day; that is paying for almost nothing but idle hours.

choices.text: App Runner, since its instances sleep between calls
choices.why: It is closed to new customers, and between calls it still pays memory for every provisioned instance.

choices.text: Lambda
choices.why: Right. About 152,000 requests a month cost cents as functions; every other option pays for the hours nobody calls.

choices.text: Two c7g.large instances, the smallest that are not burstable
choices.why: That is 162.21 a month, the dearest option on every small profile.

prompt: An application is moving from EC2 to Lambda. Which of its habits have to change before it can move? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which assume a machine that stays, a process that stays, or a lot of time?

choices.text: It keeps user sessions in the process's memory
choices.why: Each concurrent request can land in a different environment, and an environment can vanish.

choices.text: It writes uploaded files to its local disk
choices.why: /tmp lasts one execution environment; the files have to go to S3 or EFS.

choices.text: It runs a twenty-minute reconciliation every night
choices.why: That is past the 900-second limit; it has to be split or moved to a task.

choices.text: It reads its configuration from environment variables
choices.why: Functions have environment variables too; this habit travels as it is.

choices.text: It is written in Python
choices.why: Python is a managed Lambda runtime; the language is not the obstacle.

prompt: The steady profile carries 78.84 million requests a month. If each request ran 50 ms instead of 100, still in 512 MB on Arm (0.2 USD per million requests, 0.0000133334 USD per GB-second), what would Lambda cost a month, in USD, to the cent?
hint: One request is now 0.05 s × 0.5 GB of GB-seconds.

prompt: Put the four options for the nightly profile in order, from the cheapest to the dearest, as compare.py priced them.
hint: Twenty-two silent hours a day.
trap: Putting Fargate before App Runner forgets that App Runner pays memory alone in the silent hours.

prompt: Writing down the requests per second for each hour of an ordinary day gives the service's request ___.
hint: Twenty-four numbers, one per hour.
